title: Network Model
description: Explain CODASYL owner/member sets, navigational access, multiple relationship roles, and association records, with SQL mirrors that distinguish shared links from ownership violations.
notes:
## Linking records through named relationships

The network data model associated with CODASYL organizes records through explicitly defined relationship sets. A set type relates an owner record type to a member record type. A set occurrence contains a particular owner and its related member occurrences under the supported membership rules. The word set here names a database relationship construct rather than simply any unordered mathematical collection.

Unlike a basic hierarchical tree, a record can participate in several named relationship roles. It might be a member in one set and an owner in another, or a member in several different set types. That gives the model more relationship flexibility than a single-parent containment tree. The exact membership, insertion, and removal rules still belong to the particular schema and product.

IDMS is a well-known implementation associated with network database concepts. This topic explains the classical owner/member model rather than claiming to implement its full native interface in MySQL. The SQL exercises represent relationship facts in ordinary tables so the structural ideas can be tested without executing an IDMS program or changing a real network schema.

## Distinguishing a set type from an occurrence

A SupplierParts set type describes a relationship between supplier and part-related records. One occurrence concerns a particular supplier and its members. Another occurrence can concern a different supplier. The definition describes permitted structure, while actual occurrences identify which records participate. A diagram of two types does not mean only two records exist.

A member's participation must be interpreted for the particular set type. In the simplified conventional ownership model used here, a member belongs to at most one owner occurrence for a given set type. The same member can participate through a different set type with a different owner role. Multiple named relationships are not the same as arbitrary multiple owners within one relationship.

Optionality also matters. A supported schema can define whether membership is required or optional and how a record becomes connected. Do not assume every record must immediately appear in every possible set merely because it has the corresponding type. The actual implementation must enforce the intended membership and lifecycle rules.

## Following navigational access

Classical network access is often navigational. A program locates a record and follows a supported set relationship, using operations appropriate to its database interface. Product documentation includes operations such as finding an owner within a set. The application needs an understanding of the schema and current navigation context to request the intended related records.

This can fit repetitive relationship traversals well. A task beginning with one warehouse and visiting its related stock records follows a known path. The same application may need different navigation or access support for a new report across all suppliers. The trade-off is between explicit path control and the flexibility of describing a desired result independently of a predefined traversal.

Do not infer that every operation requires a linear pointer walk or that indexes and direct access are impossible. Actual products can offer several access mechanisms and additional query interfaces. The model's navigational tradition explains a common application dependency, not an exhaustive restriction on every implementation bearing the network label.

## Interpreting several owner roles carefully

Suppose a Part occurrence participates in a SupplierHome set and a WarehouseHome set. It can have an owner playing the supplier role and another playing the warehouse role. This is a useful contrast with a simple containment tree because the record participates in two independently named relationships.

That illustration does not by itself establish unrestricted many-to-many supply and stocking. If the business says a part can have many suppliers and each supplier can supply many parts, one direct single-owner membership cannot express all those associations. Likewise, many warehouses stocking the same part require a representation that preserves several distinct stocking facts.

A model should not claim to solve a many-to-many requirement merely because a record has two differently typed owners. The two relationships might each still be one-to-many. State the actual cardinality of each requirement and identify whether the representation can express every allowed combination without duplicating the part's identity.

## Using association records for repeated relationships

An association record can represent a supply fact linking a supplier and a part. It can participate as a member in a supplier-owned set and a part-owned set, letting the same association be reached through either relationship. Several association occurrences can then represent several suppliers for one part and several parts for one supplier.

Attributes such as quoted price or delivery lead time belong to the association when they describe a particular supplier-part relationship. Putting one price directly on Part would lose the distinction between suppliers if their offers differ. This is a modeling issue about which fact owns the attribute, not just a matter of choosing a pointer direction.

The association needs its own identity and duplicate policy. If only one current supply fact is allowed per supplier-part pair, duplicate occurrences should be rejected or consolidated under an explicit rule. If historical offers are required, time or another occurrence identifier may distinguish them. The relationship structure does not automatically invent the missing temporal semantics.

## Managing change and lifecycle

Connecting, disconnecting, inserting, or deleting records can affect set membership. A product's schema rules determine whether a member may exist independently and what happens when an owner is removed. Do not assume that every owner deletion automatically destroys all related entities. A shared part's identity can differ from the lifecycle of one supplier's supply association.

Application code may depend on particular set names and traversal sequences. Renaming or reorganizing those paths can require caller changes even when the visible business labels stay similar. Inspect the actual record definitions, access programs, and supported migration procedure before making a structural change in a real network database.

This is the navigational coupling often contrasted with relational declarative access. It is a useful design consideration, not a claim that all network databases are obsolete or that every relational query is automatically independent of physical and logical choices. Both approaches need accurate contracts and verified compatibility during change.

## Comparing with modern graph terminology

Network databases and graph databases both discuss connected records, but the similarity does not make their models interchangeable. Classical CODASYL sets have defined owner/member roles and membership rules. Modern graph products can use property graphs, other graph models, and query languages with different relationship semantics. Their constraint and schema capabilities vary by product.

Avoid the oversimplification that every graph database is schema-free and every network database has only one access style. Compare the actual identity, cardinality, navigation, query, and integrity requirements. A drawing containing circles and arrows cannot establish compatibility between two engines with very different object and operation contracts.

For a supplier question, ask whether the model can represent all required associations and attributes, how the query reaches them, and which rules protect shared identity. Those concrete questions reveal more than choosing a model because the word network sounds similar to graph.

## Auditing a relational mirror of membership

A teaching table can record set_name, owner_id, and member_id. Under the stated simplified rule, a member may have one owner per set name while appearing in another named role. A query listing the relationships of one member demonstrates that distinction without requiring a native database traversal API.

A raw import ledger can deliberately allow several candidate rows so a second query finds ownership conflicts. Count distinct owners per set and member. Repeated copies of the same owner relation should not be mistaken for two different owners, while one member linked to two owners within the same constrained set should be flagged. Membership in two different sets is not that violation.

This audit tests the declared fixture policy, not actual IDMS enforcement. A row in an ordinary MySQL table does not create a CODASYL set occurrence in another engine. Native membership operations, transaction behavior, and access performance remain separate verification questions. Naming that scope keeps practical SQL practice honest.

The network model is useful for understanding explicit relationships beyond basic tree containment. Keep set types, occurrences, owner roles, and association facts distinct. Define cardinality and lifecycle rules before choosing paths, and verify the real implementation separately from a teaching mirror. Those distinctions make the model a precise account of relationships rather than an unsupported promise that every connected diagram expresses the same facts.

questions.question_text: What CODASYL-defined construct represents a relationship between an owner record type and member record types in the network model?
options: A join table
A set
A collection
An index
questions.explanation: The CODASYL network model organizes relationships into named 'sets', each with one owner record type and one or more member record types.

questions.question_text: What flexibility does the classical network model add beyond a basic single-parent tree?
options: It eliminates the need for pointers
A record can participate in several named set types and owner/member roles
It uses SQL for querying
It requires no schema design at all
questions.explanation: This does not imply arbitrary multiple owners within one constrained set type.

questions.question_text: Which system is a well-known industrial implementation of the CODASYL network model?
options: IDMS
MongoDB
Neo4j
Cassandra
questions.explanation: IDMS (Integrated Database Management System) was a widely deployed CODASYL network-model database used in enterprise mainframe systems.

questions.question_text: How does an application typically retrieve data from a CODASYL network database?
options: Declarative SQL SELECT statements
Procedural navigation using DML calls like FIND and FIND NEXT WITHIN a named set
Automatic schema-free document queries
REST API calls
questions.explanation: CODASYL databases use navigational DML where the program explicitly finds owner records and walks member chains within named sets.

questions.question_text: Part participates in a supplier-owned set and a warehouse-owned set. What does that establish?
options: Parts cannot be shared between sets
Participation in two differently named relationships, not automatically unrestricted many-to-many cardinality
This is only possible in relational databases
Sets can only have one member record type
questions.explanation: Many-to-many facts may need association records.

questions.question_text: What dependency can make changes to a navigational network schema costly?
options: It could not represent one-to-many relationships
Programs can depend on defined set paths and navigation context
It could not run on mainframes
It required a graph query language that didn't exist yet
questions.explanation: Actual products may also offer indexes and other query interfaces.

questions.question_text: How should classical CODASYL sets be compared with modern graph products?
options: They are actually identical in every respect
Compare actual relationship, constraint, and query semantics rather than assuming connected diagrams are interchangeable
Modern graph databases cannot represent many-to-many relationships
The network model uses SQL while graph databases do not
questions.explanation: Modern graph models and schema support vary by product.

questions.question_text: Which standards tradition is associated with the classical network database model?
options: ANSI
ISO
CODASYL
W3C
questions.explanation: The question identifies the tradition without relying on an unverified precise historical date.

questions.question_text: What does a set occurrence concern?
options: Every database record worldwide
A particular owner and its related members under the set rules
Only a type name with no records
A result sort order
questions.explanation: A type defines structure; an occurrence supplies actual participants.

questions.question_text: Where does a supplier-specific quoted price naturally belong in a many-to-many supply design?
options: On an unrelated warehouse label
On the database connection
On the supplier-part association fact
On the part alone regardless of supplier
questions.explanation: The measurement concerns a particular relationship.

questions.question_text: Member 10 has one owner in set A and another owner in set B. Is that automatically a one-owner-per-set violation?
options: Yes; a member can never have two relationships
Only if both owner numbers are positive
No; the roles are different set types
Only if the names are lowercase
questions.explanation: The simplified ownership rule is scoped by set type.

questions.question_text: Member 10 has owners 7 and 8 in the same constrained set A. What should the import audit flag?
options: Two valid unrelated set names
A necessarily duplicated part name
A missing timestamp only
An ownership conflict for set A and member 10
questions.explanation: Two distinct owners violate the stated one-owner-per-set policy.

questions.question_text: Two raw ledger rows repeat the same owner relation. Why count DISTINCT owner_id for the ownership conflict?
options: Duplicate copies do not imply different owners
Every duplicate is a different physical entity
COUNT(*) always means distinct owners
Grouping removes all duplicates automatically
questions.explanation: The audit is about owner cardinality, not raw row copies.

questions.question_text: A part has many suppliers and each supplier has many parts. What representation can preserve the individual supply facts?
options: One unrestricted name field
Association records connected through supplier and part roles
One supplier pointer with no other facts
Copy every part without identity review
questions.explanation: Association occurrences represent repeated relationships explicitly.

questions.question_text: An owner is deleted. Which behavior cannot be assumed from the model label alone?
options: That a relationship definition matters
That the operation has an owner
That every related shared entity is automatically deleted
That lifecycle rules need review
questions.explanation: The actual schema and operation define the lifecycle.

questions.question_text: A native navigation program depends on a named set path. What might a path reorganization require?
options: Only a different diagram color
No change under every implementation
Automatic migration of all programs
Caller and compatibility review
questions.explanation: Navigation dependencies can be observable application contracts.

questions.question_text: A MySQL query audits set_name rows successfully. What remains unverified?
options: Native IDMS membership enforcement and performance
The fixture query result
That synthetic rows were evaluated
That the SQL executed on its recorded engine
questions.explanation: A relational mirror does not run another engine's native operations.

questions.question_text: A graph product supports schema constraints. Does that contradict an accurate comparison with CODASYL?
options: Yes; every graph must be schema-free
No; graph products have varied model and constraint capabilities
Only if it has no edges
Only if it lacks SQL
questions.explanation: Avoid treating all modern graph products as one unconstrained model.

questions.question_text: A warehouse query repeatedly follows a known set path. What determines whether it is efficient?
options: The word network alone
The count of arrows in a picture
The actual access mechanism, data, and workload
The absence of relational tables everywhere
questions.explanation: Model vocabulary is not a performance measurement.

questions.question_text: Supply offers need historical prices. What must identity design distinguish?
options: Only the current part name
Only the number of owners in another set
Only the server port
Different offer occurrences or times for the supplier-part pair
questions.explanation: Repeated relationship facts may need temporal identity rather than accidental duplicates.

coding_problems.title: List a member across named relationship roles
coding_problems.task: In the relational network mirror, return set_name and owner_id for member_id 10, ordered by set_name. The unique key permits one owner per set/member pair. Different set names represent different roles. This does not execute native network-database operations.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE memberships (set_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, owner_id INT NOT NULL, member_id INT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(set_name,member_id));
constraints: One owner per named set/member pair
The mirror omits native navigation and lifecycle rules
edge_cases: One member can participate in different sets
An absent member returns no rows
hints: Do not merge different set names
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT set_name,owner_id FROM memberships WHERE member_id=10 ORDER BY set_name;
coding_problems.explanation: The output preserves distinct relationship roles for the same member under the stated fixture policy.

coding_problems.title: Find conflicting owner assignments in an import
coding_problems.task: Audit raw_links for violations of the fixture rule: at most one distinct owner per set_name and member_id. Return set_name, member_id, owner_count for groups with more than one distinct owner, ordered by set_name then member_id. Duplicate copies of one owner relation are not ownership conflicts.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE raw_links (link_id INT PRIMARY KEY, set_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, owner_id INT NOT NULL, member_id INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Raw rows intentionally allow conflicting candidates
This is an import audit, not an actual grant or native set mutation
edge_cases: Repeated same-owner rows are not conflicts
More than two owners must all be counted
hints: Group by the full relationship scope
Use COUNT(DISTINCT owner_id) in both output and HAVING
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT set_name,member_id,COUNT(DISTINCT owner_id) AS owner_count FROM raw_links GROUP BY set_name,member_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT owner_id)>1 ORDER BY set_name,member_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The grouping scopes ownership to a named set and member. Distinct counting separates different owners from duplicate import copies.

original_questions.question_text: What CODASYL-defined construct represents a relationship between an owner record type and member record types in the network model?
options: A join table
A set
A collection
An index
original_questions.explanation: The CODASYL network model organizes relationships into named 'sets', each with one owner record type and one or more member record types.

original_questions.question_text: What is the key structural improvement the network model offers over the hierarchical model?
options: It eliminates the need for pointers
A member record can belong to multiple sets, i.e., have more than one owner
It uses SQL for querying
It requires no schema design at all
original_questions.explanation: Unlike hierarchical trees where each record has exactly one parent, network model records can be members of multiple sets, natively supporting many-to-many relationships.

original_questions.question_text: Which system is a well-known industrial implementation of the CODASYL network model?
options: IDMS
MongoDB
Neo4j
Cassandra
original_questions.explanation: IDMS (Integrated Database Management System) was a widely deployed CODASYL network-model database used in enterprise mainframe systems.

original_questions.question_text: How does an application typically retrieve data from a CODASYL network database?
options: Declarative SQL SELECT statements
Procedural navigation using DML calls like FIND and FIND NEXT WITHIN a named set
Automatic schema-free document queries
REST API calls
original_questions.explanation: CODASYL databases use navigational DML where the program explicitly finds owner records and walks member chains within named sets.

original_questions.question_text: In a network model schema where Part is a member of both a 'supplies' set (owned by Supplier) and a 'stocks' set (owned by Warehouse), what does this demonstrate?
options: Parts cannot be shared between sets
A record can have multiple owners, solving the many-to-many limitation of hierarchical trees
This is only possible in relational databases
Sets can only have one member record type
original_questions.explanation: Part participating in two sets shows the network model's core advantage: a member record can be linked to multiple distinct owners.

original_questions.question_text: What is a major drawback of the network model that ultimately motivated the shift to the relational model?
options: It could not represent one-to-many relationships
All access paths (sets) must be predefined in the schema, and application code is tightly coupled to that pointer structure
It could not run on mainframes
It required a graph query language that didn't exist yet
original_questions.explanation: Because traversal paths are hard-coded as sets and navigated procedurally, unanticipated queries or schema changes required redesigning both schema and application code.

original_questions.question_text: How does the CODASYL network model fundamentally differ from a modern graph database like Neo4j, despite both using 'nodes and connections'?
options: They are actually identical in every respect
The network model uses rigid, schema-predefined sets navigated procedurally, while modern graph databases use a flexible property graph with declarative query languages
Modern graph databases cannot represent many-to-many relationships
The network model uses SQL while graph databases do not
original_questions.explanation: Network model sets are fixed at schema design time and walked with procedural code, whereas graph databases allow new relationship types at runtime and support declarative traversal languages like Cypher.

original_questions.question_text: Which organization standardized the network data model in the late 1960s?
options: ANSI
ISO
CODASYL
W3C
original_questions.explanation: CODASYL (Conference on Data Systems Languages) produced the specification that defined the network data model, hence it is often called the CODASYL model.

diagrams.caption: Two owner roles versus an ownership conflict
diagrams.description: The simplified rule allows one owner per set type and member. Two different set names are separate roles, while two distinct owners in the same constrained set/member scope conflict.
rows: A different role, not a conflict
Conflicts if that set permits only one owner
